title: Dr Dewi Evans, Dr Sandie Bohin, Claire Hocknell, Summary of interview with Lucy Letby

blocks.text: 18 November 2022
Baby E
DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
DR SANDIE BOHIN (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Questions from THE JUDGE
MRS CLAIRE HOCKNELL (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby E] (read)
Friday, 18 November 2022
(In the presence of the jury)
Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, Dr Dewi Evans, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Dr Evans. For the recording would you identify yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes: Dr Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Have you written several reports bearing on the case of [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was your initial sift report dated 7 November 2017?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your more substantive report, dated 31 May 2018?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And did you then provide three further statements or reports, dated 24 January 2019, first of all?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: March, 24 March.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I beg your pardon, 24 March.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 2019. Did that deal -- well, I'll deal with the material in a moment.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was there then a statement dated 15 October 2021?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, there was a little one on 24 June 2021 -- 15 October 2021, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. The one I had finally was -- the version I have doesn't bear the date, but that's the June 2021 statement.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. Can we deal first with the material that you received. As in other cases, did you receive from the police medical records from the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A selection of which the jury has seen as the evidence has been deployed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you also receive material from Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Some photographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And radiographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: At a later stage, in 2019, when you made your statement in 2019, were you sent extracts from witness statements that had been made by some of the witnesses?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And in particular, were you sent an extract from [Mother of Babies E & F]'s witness statement --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- concerning the events that she told the jury about in evidence on Monday of this week?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Has all that material been brought to bear so far as your opinion in this case is concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it has.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to start, if we may, with your report of 31 May 2018. Within the body of the report and at the beginning of that report do you summarise the time of [Baby E]'s birth, his birth weight, the gestation at the time of his birth, and the date of his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm just going to run through quickly some of the tiles to put all this into context if we may. If Mr Murphy would help, please. Starting with tile number 5, does that record the circumstances of [Baby E]'s birth on 29 July, the material behind that tile?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I don't know what's behind it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's all right, don't worry. I'm just going to wait for Mr Murphy to click on the tile for me. If you don't mind waiting a second.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
I think that --
Yes. I can't read the small print, but yes, I'm familiar with that page.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So this deals with the admission of [Baby E] to the neonatal unit --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- which we've heard was shortly after his birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And there within your report, I think you have noted his heart rate, his sats, the fact that he was in air, and his temperature?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is that right? Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you observe that the emergency delivery of [Babies E & F] was due to in utero growth retardation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That was the information at the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And did you note the fact that the Apgar score for [Baby E] was 7 at 1 minute and 9 at 9 or 10 minutes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you record the fact that at 22.40 on the 29th, [Baby E] was recorded as "desaturating on handling"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that an umbilical venous catheter had been passed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If we just come out of that screen, please, if we could, for a moment.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as your summary was concerned, Dr Evans, did you move from the 29th to the 30th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you record the fact that [Baby E] at 9.30 that morning, on the 30th, was on CPAP in air?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you record various other findings from some sort of blood analysis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. His CRP, which is a marker of inflammation, was low, was 1, which is normal. His haemoglobin was fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: His white cells were a normal range. And also that his oxygen saturations were 100% in air. In other words, as stable as you can get.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Did you record the fact that later that morning, a long line had been inserted into his left saphenous vein?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And where is the saphenous vein?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the leg, inside of the leg.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you then observe the blood gas findings or readings at 18.21, later that day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did and they were all very satisfactory results.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Moving on to day 3 of [Baby E]'s life, 31 July 2015, did you note the fact that it had been recorded in the notes that [Baby E] had been off CPAP since midday the previous day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That his blood gases were excellent?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That he was receiving liquid feed through a line?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, intravenous fluid, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You recorded his urine output?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, which was very satisfactory, within the normal range.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And what did you observe so far as his breathing was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, his oxygen saturation was 100% in air. So he was not requiring additional oxygen. His respiratory rate was 70, and he was active and pink, so all was satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you record the fact that because [Baby E]'s glucose was raised on 31 July, he had started to receive insulin intravenously?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was that -- do you know between what times the insulin was being received by [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Now, he had insulin on and off, if I could put it that way, over the next few days. So he was started on insulin at about 6.45 in the morning because his glucose values were increased. His sugar level dropped to low volumes, so it was stopped, and then over the next few days his insulin was restarted, stopped again, restarted and stopped again. So I can go through the times when it was started, stopped, started, stopped. But on the whole, his glucose values were above the normal range during his next few days, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. If anyone wants to make a note of it, the prescription for insulin, I think, is at tile 94, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Perhaps we can stick with your summary for now and if any further detail is required it can be adduced in due course.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The total time that [Baby E] received insulin, was it just over about 3 hours that day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Initially, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that's 31 July. Moving on to day 4 for [Baby E], which was 1 August, again how was [Baby E]'s breathing on day 4?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, what I've entered from 11 am is:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Well. Good gases. No increased work of breathing."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore stable respiratory condition and he was still having a small dose of insulin from 7.30 pm on that day.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Again, if the precise time at which [Baby E] received insulin is relevant, that is recorded at tile 94, I think, or at least the prescription --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- is there recorded. So that's day 4. Day 5 of [Baby E]'s life was 2 August.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Again, he is stable. He is now on 23% oxygen.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Air is 21% oxygen, so he's on a tiny amount of oxygen and it records that his saturations were varying between the high 80s and the low 90s, which is why he would have been given a bit of oxygen in the first place to sustain satisfactory oxygen levels. The only other comment I noted was of mild recession, in other words you could see the ribs moving during his breathing. But that's pretty common in little babies anyway so that's okay.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is this what has been referred to by some of the treating professionals as subcostal recession?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you note the record of how [Baby E] was handling?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. This was a good marker, again, of well-being and they'd recorded he was moving well on handling, so that's a good sign again.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm sure the jury now are reasonably familiar with this point, but what is the point here about how babies behave when they're being handled by medical professionals or their parents?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Premature babies particularly, if they're handled and they're not very stable, they're not very well, dislike handling and it could lead to irregularities of breathing, stopping breathing, increased or decreased heart rate, a drop in oxygen saturation. In other words, all these are markers of babies not being as well as you'd like and therefore -- which is why you need to handle them as little as possible, so therefore if they're moving well on handling and they're "handling well", which is the term used, if they're handling well it means that they don't have any of these markers that suggest that there is something wrong with them or something unwell with them, I should say.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. Can we move, please, Mr Murphy, to tile 56.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could we go to the original document, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As I think everybody in this room understands, this is a document that covers a 24-hour period.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: From 18.00 hours on 2 August to 17.00 hours on 3 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If we could just scroll down a little, please, so that we can get all three lines plotted within view.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What does this tell us, if anything, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is an extremely satisfactory pattern of well-being.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The top line measures heart rate and the heart rate is -- it's a snapshot every hour of the heart rate.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: [Baby E] would be on continuous heart rate monitoring.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But this is the snapshot taken by the nursing staff every hour and all heart rate values are normal, they're around about 140, one or two go up to 150, but this is a very, very stable pattern.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The second one relates to his respiratory rate.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Initially, it was 70, which is at the top end of the normal range. You know, above 60 is -- sorry, up to 60 is considered the normal range. But it settles down very, very quickly and his respiratory rate is around about 50 for most of that day. Then his temperature is within the normal range. So in other words, that's fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that's the 24 hours approaching the night shift on which he died?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can we just look at tile 71 as well, which deals with — if we just hold that for a second, just to put this into context. We can see 10 o'clock, 10 am, on the 3rd marked there, can't we, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 10 o'clock, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That column that's being highlighted now by, very helpfully, by Mr Murphy. Just to take an example of something else going on at the same time, if we can go to tile 71, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we look to the right-hand side of that document, we see:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Kangaroo care for mum and dad."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: For 3 hours as recorded from 10 am, so that takes us from 10 until 1 pm.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've heard direct evidence from [Nurse B] about that, so you told us what the charts show us. The charts in conjunction with the evidence given by [Nurse B], what does that show us?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is the kangaroo care record. Kangaroo care is where the baby's brought out and nursed, held by its mum. And again, you'd only consider kangaroo care once the baby is stable because, as we've heard, if babies are handled and they're unwell they don't -- they can deteriorate. Therefore the presence of kangaroo care and that he was coping with kangaroo care meant that he was a very stable, well little baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you. Tile 78, if we could move on to that and look at a different source of information during this threehour period from 10 until 1.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 11.45 we have Dr Ventress' notes from the ward round. She told us, I believe, in evidence that [Baby E] was having skinto-skin with [Mother of Babies E & F] at this stage.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Well, it's not on the note, but yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, that was the evidence.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you remember --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ah yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- the other doctor who came later, the blonde lady whose name I've temporarily forgotten, told us that she examined [Baby E] later because there hadn't been an examination at this stage.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was having cuddles with mum.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Exactly. This note also shows, I believe, that [Baby E] was spontaneously ventilating in 25% oxygen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So again, is that a sign of well-being?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Very well, he's breathing without support, needing little whiff of oxygen. That's fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Moving on to tile 86, please. This is the lady whose name I'd forgotten, Dr Thomas. Her examination at 14.10. We can see the fact that there was a physical examination is there recorded by her.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "No suspicious aspirates, abdomen not distended, and handling appropriately throughout the day with no increased work of breathing."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's recorded by Dr Thomas. So this is just after the three-hour period of kangaroo care recorded by [Nurse B].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So again, what does this source of information reveal?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, he's coped with his kangaroo care, he's coped with the handling involved with kangaroo care, his condition is extremely stable, his heart rate findings are normal, his oxygen saturations are satisfactory and there aren't any abdominal concerns -- you know, there's no abdominal distension, bowels not opened yet, pretty much -- quite common in little babies. But he's got "BS present", bowel sounds present, so a good sign, normal sign, and no suspicious aspirates, which relate to -- if a baby's intestines aren't working very well, you'll get aspirates up the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So a very, very stable little baby and AF, anterior fontanelle, soft, ie normal.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We can see in Dr Thomas' plan that because the abdominal examination had been normal, the feeds could be increased?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Can go up on feeds."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on to tile 90, please. Actually, I think it's there, I think it's on this piece of paper as well, so rather than... Yes, just looking at this, we can see at the bottom that the blood sugar was elevated at 18.4?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And therefore the plan was to restart insulin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A very small dose because one of the previous doses had had significant results?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, previously his initial -- the first time he was started on insulin, his glucose value dropped quite quickly. So therefore this is a tiny dose. [Baby E]'s own insulin had not kicked in, obviously -- not unusual in little babies, prem babies -- so therefore, he was given, correctly, top-up insulin intravenously by infusion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Anything concerning so far as your opinion is concerned, doctor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, by this time he was well. He needed insulin to control his glucose values, that is fine, that's what neonatal units are for. So that was the -- so that's fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on to after 6 pm, so approaching the night shift. I'm going to move to tile 106, please. This is the chart for the next 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's J2685 if anyone wants to make a note.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Here we see, Dr Evans, the time parameters set out along the top row: 18.00 hours to 00.15, rolling over into 4 August.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just in general terms for now, if you would, please, what does that -- what does the data on that chart show?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. The top record is the heart rate and it's a continuation of the chart we saw a few minutes ago.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So from 18.00 hours until 21.00 hours, heart rate remains nice and stable at around 140. Similarly for his respiratory rate from 18.00 hours to 21.00 hours, a nice and stable respiratory rate, 40 to 50 per minute, and temperature normal. So therefore, during the first part of the evening, we've got very stable results.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we go next, please, to tile 128.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Here we have, first of all, Dr Thomas' notes made just before the shift handover.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is there anything at all concerning in Dr Thomas' notes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. From the top, no is the answer, because -- right, his CRP is less than 1. It tends to -- which is a very encouraging finding. His white cells, again, 3.6 from 6.3. Both of those values are within normal values.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: BM is now settling. The BM is the glucose value, so it's 12.1, 12.8, so above the normal range, but a value of 12 would be satisfactory. It's not going to cause the baby any harm. The plan was to repeat the glucose in 4 hours. That's fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: These results show that they were planning to stop the antibiotics at 36 hours because he was improving.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: No -- I can't read that, something CRP. And the blood cultures were negative to date. In other words that's
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "BC negative to date", that's blood culture, and blood cultures, you check every baby for infection, so the blood cultures were negative, which is excellent, and so yes, all well.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. Can we move next to the fluid balance chart at tile 121, which is J2720.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we highlight, please, Mr Murphy, the columns 20.15 to 22.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just looking back along the feeds row or rows, please, Dr Evans, do we see that [Baby E] was being fed via his nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Initially, from 01.00 hours up to and including 13.00 hours, so in other words, a 12-hour period?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was he receiving a single millilitre of breast milk every 2 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: From 15.00 hours do we see those feeds, those bihourly feeds, being increased or doubled to 2ml every 2 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: From 13.00 hours, actually, yes, it went up to 2ml twohourly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think it's actually, with respect, I think it's 15.00.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh it is, sorry, yes. Apologies. I can't read that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, sorry.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Don't worry. Then we see that, according to Lucy Letby's note, that feed was omitted at 21.00 hours and we have various notes relating to a "mucky 16ml", the word "discarded", and then in the 22.00 hours section we can see "6ml blood" written in.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's 15ml fresh blood and 6ml blood, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you. We know from the evidence of Dr Harkness that he was called to see [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That information is recorded in his notes at tile 124, if we could go there, please. So this is the bottom half of the same page we were looking at earlier:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Attend] to see patient re gastric bleed."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And we heard the evidence that he gave yesterday.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, we did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: [Baby E] was treated with ranitidine --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- which is designed to deal with stomach acid problems; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And with an antibiotic, is it metronidazole?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Metronidazole, yes. Yes, it's a specialist antibiotic, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That particular antibiotic, he told us, is designed to deal with what?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It deals with what we call anaerobic organisms and you introduce metronidazole if you suspect necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Those were the events at 22.10. At tile 140 we have Dr Harkness' notes dealing with the blood loss at 23.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If we could just look at that, please. It's the one further down the page, I'm sorry. 23.00 hours, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do we there see Dr Harkness' record of the events about which he told us yesterday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We see towards the middle of that entry:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Saturates remained 60 to 70% in 100% oxygen."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But underneath that, the line:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Making good respiratory effort. Crying."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We'll come back to that when we come to your opinions, Dr Evans, if we may.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Moving on to tile 199 next, please. Do we there have -- I think these are the consultant's records; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think so, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do we there see a record of [Baby E]'s collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Gastrointestinal haemorrhage. Discoloured abdomen."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the material that we were told about in evidence over the last couple of days?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'd like to move on to your observations, please, Dr Evans, which are set out from paragraph 14 onwards of your report.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've heard something of the circumstances which led to [Mother of Babies E & F] receiving a caesarean section at Chester.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The particular problems or prenatal problems that [Baby E], taken as an individual, had suffered, what would they have had on his lungs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. [Baby E] was one of twins, so therefore he had to share with his twin. But the antenatal records had recorded this phenomenon of absent or reverse end-diastolic flow, which is a marker of placental insufficiency.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just to stop you there, I'm sorry. What does placental insufficiency mean?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Placental insufficiency means that the baby is not -- is at risk because if the placenta isn't working very well, then there is a risk that the baby is compromised and not receiving adequate oxygenation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. So that's the potential problem that's been flagged?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And what do those circumstances -- what impact do they have on a baby's lungs and their capacity to breathe when born?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Perversely, this will stress the baby and this leads to improving the baby's lungs to breathe out of utero. In other words, it's nature's way of preparing the baby to breathe outside the womb, I suppose, in a simple way.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore you can often find that babies who have evidence of end-diastolic flow abnormality, in other words placenta not quite working as well as it should be, remarkably they tend to do quite well breathing-wise once they are born, which is what happened to [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He required hardly any breathing support at all.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's -- which is great.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. So what one might expect from this particular set of circumstances in fact materialised as reflected in the
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: evidence of those who cared for [Baby E] between 29 July and 3 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, that's right. In other words, they will be prepared to -- sorry, they would anticipate that if [Baby E] had significant breathing problems then you might require CPAP and if CPAP was insufficient, more oxygen, and if that -- sorry, if that was insufficient you'd require ventilatory support. In other words, the baby would be placed on a breathing machine, on a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: None of this was required, which is great, which is very satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You have touched on this to a degree already, but [Baby E]'s high blood sugar, what was the cause of that, first of all?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. A straightforward cause of [Baby E]'s blood sugar is that his insulin production, his own insulin production, had not kicked in. In other words, you need to produce insulin from the pancreas to regulate glucose values or sugar values. So he's a prem baby, so [Baby E]'s particular problem was that his own insulin had not -- was insufficient to stabilise his glucose values and therefore he required top-up insulin intravenously.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've heard that [Dr C], the consultant, ultimately took the view at the time that [Baby E] suffered with or from NEC.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: First of all, is that a problem that is associated with the circumstances that faced [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Why is that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: He's at increased risk of NEC. I said earlier that the placental insufficiency had a beneficial effect regarding his breathing, but it has an increased risk of him developing necrotising enterocolitis, which is this condition that affects the small intestine and causes abdominal tenderness, bleeding from the bowel, you know, and in serious cases can cause perforation of the bowel.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore he was at increased risk of necrotising enterocolitis and therefore what the department did was keep a very careful eye on his abdominal status and one of the things they did was hold off giving oral feeds for the first few days. So therefore
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: he was at increased risk of NEC and, given what we know, he did not develop NEC.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If a baby has NEC to any significant degree, how does that usually present itself?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What you find is that the baby becomes sort of gradually unwell. You might find a bit of abdominal distension.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you place your hand on the baby's abdomen, he would -- you might detect that -- tenderness.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How does a baby, given that the baby can't speak, inform you that it's tender when you put your hand on the abdomen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: His heart rate might go up, his respiratory rate might go up, his oxygen might drop. Those are the usual markers. We've mentioned handling earlier. He would not have coped with handling in any way. So therefore those are the initial markers of NEC. They are pretty non-specific, but, you know, if you're used to dealing with premature babies you would pick up these signs of early NEC, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: On a slightly -- on the same point about NEC, is abdominal distension a well-known symptom of NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Would you expect all medical professionals from the most senior consultant to the most junior neonatal nurse to know that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In an aspirate taken from a baby with NEC, what might one expect to find?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You might expect to find bile in the aspirate and you might expect an increasing amount of aspirate. So instead of finding, you know, half a millilitre or something, which is usually of no significance, you might find 1 or 2ml and an increasing amount of aspirate from the NG tube.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Might the aspirate contain anything in addition to bile if a baby had NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the whole, no. On the whole, no. No, it's usually bile and, you know, juices, watery juices.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you, having considered all the available evidence, consider that NEC is a viable explanation for what happened to [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no. No, I've dealt with NEC on a number of occasions. [Baby E], in my opinion, did not have clinical features consistent with NEC.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I want to move next, in dealing with what was or were the cause or the causes of [Baby E]'s premature demise, to turn to what you were told about what witnesses had seen.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So for your assistance, Dr Evans, I'm going to turn to your witness statement of 24 -- in the version I have it says January, but I think you told us it's March 2019 --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- which deals with descriptions given by [Mother of Babies E & F] --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and by Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So here, to summarise the position for the jury, we're dealing with events that [Mother of Babies E & F] says happened at about 9 pm --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and which Dr Harkness tells us happened after 10 or 11 pm when he told the jury he saw this discolouration on [Baby E]'s abdomen.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So dealing with [Mother of Babies E & F]'s description, first of all, of seeing blood on [Baby E] -- I'm very much summarising now her evidence, but you as, we did, heard what she had to say about seeing blood around her son's mouth --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and hearing noises being made by her son.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What, if any, conclusion did you draw from the description given by [Mother of Babies E & F]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, this would have been completely unexpected given [Baby E]'s condition, stable condition, previously. It really would be difficult to explain how a baby has stabilised out for several days and has now got blood from its mouth and was making what we heard the other day was this horrendous noise. So this was -- it's not something I think I've seen, actually, other than this case.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Dr Harkness, as we've seen in the notes, as we've gone through, speaks of blood coming up the NG tube --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and he speaks of skin discolouration, purple patches --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- on [Baby E]'s abdomen.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Are those findings, to your mind, relevant in the context of the reason for [Baby E]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they are. Yes, they are.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What conclusions have you come to as to why it was [Baby E] died when he did?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I think there were two major issues here. The first was significant haemorrhage from the upper gastrointestinal tract. By that I mean somewhere between the mouth and the stomach, because of the description of what was described as fresh blood. So therefore something had caused this significant haemorrhage. [Baby E] lost a lot of blood in a short period of time, sufficient to destabilise him generally.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then in relation to the discolouration, I heard Dr Harkness' evidence yesterday, and again, as he said, this is something that he'd seen before. It's this very, very unusual pattern of patches, and he said they turned up in one part of the abdomen, then they were somewhere else and on his chest, and again this is a very, very peculiar form of discolouration which I have seen only in literature presentations other than in this series of cases.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So having seen this, I thought that [Baby E] had now been subjected to -- sorry, was suffering from an air embolus. And the discolouration of the abdomen and other parts of the body is a marker of an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So I think he had two major problems: the gastric haemorrhage or the upper GI haemorrhage, to be more specific, and an air embolus. This is why resuscitation was not successful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm looking at paragraph 9 of the report now. Is the passage of a nasogastric tube and irritation caused by the tube a credible explanation for blood round a baby's mouth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. This was my initial thought, that there had been some sort of trauma due to an NG tube. This was my initial thought. At the time I did not have any copies of the bits of equipment that were used at the baby unit. Various tubes come in different sizes, different thicknesses and different levels of rigidity. It's only recently that I saw which type of nasogastric tube was used at the hospital in 2015 or currently and the tube that they did use is very small and very flexible. So having seen that, I don't think it's that kind of nasogastric tube that would have caused -- well, any trauma, really. So therefore my initial thought, it was a nasogastric tube. Having seen the tube they used, it was not due to a nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So in your clinical opinion, Dr Evans, looking at all the evidence, what is the explanation for [Baby E]'s premature death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that he suffered trauma from some other form of injury. There are a number of bits of equipment on neonatal units that are relatively rigid. Plastic tubes used for suction, for instance, are much firmer than a nasogastric tube, so it could have been interference with that. In my last report I noted the -- something called an introducer. An introducer is a thin wire surrounded by plastic, which one uses to intubate a baby. That would be more than sufficient to cause trauma if it was used inappropriately.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So I cannot be 100% certain about what caused the trauma to his system, but it had to be some kind of relatively stiff something that was sufficient to cause this extraordinary bleeding.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, whatever the cause was or may have been, in your view is there a potential "innocent" explanation for this degree of bleeding?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no. The other option is that this was an ulcer, a bleeding ulcer. I have never seen a bleeding ulcer causing this sort of presentation. When he was born, there were stress issues
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: in relation to [Baby E]. All of those markers had long gone. In other words he was a stable baby by -- just before all of this occurred.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore whatever stresses he had experienced because of placenta not working properly and being preterm, you know, those are in themselves stress factors, all of those factors had stabilised out and were not -- and showed that he was not a baby at that time experiencing stress.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Wait there just a second. Those are all the questions I have for you. Thank you, Dr Evans. If you'd remain there, please.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You do not get delayed stress turning up out of the blue at day 5 or day 6.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no. I'm a clinician, we base our opinions on the information available to us. The information available to me initially was less than what I've heard since, so everything I've heard since adds to my initial opinion that [Baby E] was subject to trauma.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, you understand the suggestion I'm making is you're taking a rather more active role in this than that and you are actively trying to find things that would support this allegation, even where there is no evidential allegation for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby E] had a massive haemorrhage from his upper GI system. And this is not something that occurs as a result of some kind of natural phenomenon.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, when you came to make your statement, the most recent one on 13 September 2022 -- I'd like you to go to that, please, it's the second page.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, which statement is this?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's 13 September 2022.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay, got it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as statements are concerned, up to this point we'd had the first two statements where you'd had the clinical notes and you'd concluded that you could not explain the cause of the haemorrhage and, in the absence of a post-mortem, it wasn't possible to say whether he had sustained trauma. You'd already said that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We then, in March 2019, had the proposal that an NG tube could have been used. When we get to this report on 13 September 2022, you begin with this at paragraph 6, page 5400:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "In an earlier statement I queried whether [Baby E]'s haemorrhage was the result of trauma caused by inappropriate handling from a nasogastric tube, but later dismissed this suggestion as the nasogastric tubes in use are too soft to cause damage to tissue."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you say, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is absolutely correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You then turned your mind to consider something that had been brought to you by the police shortly before you wrote this report; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's referred to in paragraphs 2 and 3.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But in early October, the police brought to you something called a tracheal intubation stylet, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's a very narrow device that's used to help insert a tube, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Sometimes caused an introducer; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you said this at paragraph 7, that you remained of the view that [Baby E]'s massive haemorrhage could be due to trauma but you were unable to reach a view regarding a potential cause.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You then said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[You] have now received a tracheal intubation stylet."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you describe it. You say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It is used as an introducer when a baby requires endotracheal intubation. It consists of a stiff but flexible wire coated in plastic. For intubation purposes it is inserted inside an endotracheal tube creating sufficient rigidity to allow the successful insertion of nan endotracheal tube through the vocal cords. It is then withdrawn and discarded."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Paragraph 8 you said this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "An introducer of this nature is sufficiently rigid to traumatise a small baby's upper gastrointestinal system."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You then said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I remain of the view [Baby E]'s demise was the result of a combination of an air embolus and acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage. I am also of the view the haemorrhage may be the result of some sort of trauma to his upper gastrointestinal system."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I have put all of that in so we have everything you have said. But I want to come to the paragraph I want to ask you about, Dr Evans, given my questions. You said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I have not seen any statement noting the presence of an introducer. Therefore my opinion regarding a potential cause of his trauma must remain speculative."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "I believe it is reasonable to contemplate the possibility if a member of staff recalls that a redundant introducer was present around the time of [Baby E]'s haemorrhage. I believe it is an option that is worth exploring."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: First of all, there's absolutely no evidential basis for what you've said there, is there, in terms of the use of an introducer, from what we know at that time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I wasn't there. It was something -- it could have been an introducer, it could have been some other form of reasonably rigid piece of plastic available on a neonatal unit. So an introducer is one option. I've not gone further than discussing it as a possibility.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If it's not an introducer, it could have been a suction tube. I can't take it any further than that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The only thing you're talking about at that time is an introducer, isn't it? This is a couple of weeks before this trial started.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, yes, I'm fully aware of that. That is what I received. I only received them on 2 September. So yes, just before this trial.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You were aware of the possible things that could be used from the outset of these reports, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I had no idea what was -- I'm familiar obviously with what are used, but, you know, as to what caused this trauma, what kind of instrument, let's call it this trauma, my opinion was that [Baby E]'s bleeding was due to trauma, but I could not explain how.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: At this point, a few weeks before the trial, coming up with this statement, you were then beginning to engage in speculation as to what has happened, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, my role is to form an opinion as to what could have caused the bleeding. I changed my mind about the NG tube, having seen one, and introduced the suggestion with the introducer, and mentioned earlier other items that are fairly rigid and plastic. So those are the options. Those are the -sorry, those are the possibilities.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You start on that paragraph, I'll remind you, by saying:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I have not seen any statement noting the presence of an introducer, therefore my opinion regarding a potential cause of his trauma must remain speculative."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you said, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And rather than engaging in presenting an objective independent view on the facts we have, you are beginning to speculate with this, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, I am trying to assist the court in giving an opinion as to what could have caused a massive haemorrhage in a little baby who up until then was nice and stable.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You said, and I'll remind us because I have only read it once:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "If a member of staff recalls that a redundant introducer was present around the time of [Baby E]'s haemorrhage, I believe it is an option that's worth exploring."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "If a member of staff recalls..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that suggesting an enquiry that could be made to go around members of staff just to see if anyone can recall it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no. The police are responsible for this investigation, not me.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, what was the point of saying:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "If a member of staff recalls that an introducer was present"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What was that aimed at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because people recall these things.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Followed by:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I believe it is an option that is worth exploring"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You were just suggesting speculative enquiries to hunt around for something to support your theory?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not a theory. What we need to do is to form an opinion, the members of the jury need to form an opinion, what on earth caused this massive haemorrhage in this little baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When you say --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, 5 years ago to this month, I raised the issue that his bleed may be the result of trauma; okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's where I was then.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I believe it is an option that is worth exploring."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You are stepping outside the active facts, Dr Evans, and you are beginning to propose means of enquiry or investigation to support an allegation, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I disagree.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Whose idea was it that you should have this introducer?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I asked for the -- to see the bits of equipment.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you asked for it. Having received it, you then say to the prosecution, in the first instance, that this could be an option worth exploring; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, that is my view, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you, in doing that, Dr Evans, are involved in seeking to pursue aspects of an investigation rather than simply giving an independent opinion, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You agree, as you said in the first two reports, do you still, that the cause of death was acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it is a significant contributory factor. But if one accepts the evidence of Dr Harkness yesterday, I think air embolus was an even more significant factor and it is what precipitated his final demise.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that depends upon, of course, the situation and the view taken of what he said in his statement some years after the clinical notes, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's what he said yesterday and it's what he said in his statement.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But not what he said in his clinical notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. The absence of a post-mortem is a serious failing in this case, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the fact remains that in the absence of a postmortem, it cannot be said what the cause of the gastrointestinal haemorrhage was, can it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

Whilst you cannot say what the cause of the GI haemorrhage was, is there any evidence that you have seen to suggest it was a natural cause?

blocks.text: Yes, I did.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that was subsequently discontinued the next day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: According to the nursing records, yes.

blocks.text: No new nasogastric tube, although the nursing records state that they were unable to insert a tube into the right nostril, so I can assume that they must have tried to do that first, were unsuccessful, and therefore at the same time inserted one into the left nostril, but I can't find any record of a second nasogastric tube ever being inserted.

blocks.text: So putting that in rather more straightforward terms, there is nothing in the records to suggest any tube, for example, being inserted on 3 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh no, no. No.

blocks.text: It was the original tube so far as the records suggest --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: -- dating from 29 July?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: I don't think any of this material is controversial in the light of the cross-examination of Dr Evans, so I'll summarise it, if I may. Did you record the insertion of a line, a long line, into [Baby E]'s left long saphenous vein on 30 July?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That was withdrawn by 3 centimetres following an X-ray?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Have you recently gone back to the insulin records to establish with as much certainty as possible when and how much insulin [Baby E] was given?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I have, because the other day, during other witnesses' evidence, it became a bit confusing as to when the insulin was started and stopped and the infusions, unfortunately, are on a variety of charts throughout the bundle, so just for clarity in my own mind I went back to have a look at when the insulin was started and stopped.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. That dose was 0.02 units, so less than half of the dose that he'd been given before.

blocks.text: And on 3 August, was [Baby E] given insulin from 15.30 hours to some time shortly before his death in the early hours of the 4th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon. 0.02 units per kilogram per hour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
