blocks.text: Thank you. At 22.21 you record the blood gas results.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They are those that appear at tile 130.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do they show any abnormalities?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They show signs of a respiratory acidosis, so the pH is low, lower than it had been, the CO2 is raised, the metabolic component, ie the base excess, is normal. The glucose is up a little bit at 10.6 but not anything really to worry about. And the lactate is normal. At that stage there's a haemoglobin on the gas, which is 185 grams, which is normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So just as a word of explanation, because we've come across these terms before. In terms of acidosis, that's an increased acidity in the body; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: An increased acidity, yes, and a reduction in the pH.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the lower the pH, the more acid, the higher the pH, the more alkaline?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What's the difference between a metabolic and a respiratory acidosis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A respiratory acidosis means there's something going on with your breathing and in order to get a rise in CO2, that means that you're not getting rid of waste gases in the way you should have. So for some reason your breathing is compromised and that allows the waste gas to build up. And if that builds up, that causes a respiratory acidosis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A metabolic acidosis is anything other than a non-respiratory cause. There are lots of potential causes of metabolic acidosis, none of them [Baby E] had.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think you record, as did Dr Evans, the fact that [Baby E] was noted to be crying at 11 pm; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm moving on to your paragraph 4.23 now, please, Dr Bohin. Do you record that at 23.40, there was a sudden deterioration in [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If the jury want the reference for this, this is tile 149. The heart rate was low, a bradycardia between 80 and 90 beats per minute?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And low saturations of 60%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And at that stage, [Baby E]'s perfusion was poor, so he wasn't a pink baby, putting it in perhaps everyday terms, and his abdomen developed what Dr Harkness was telling us about yesterday in terms of discolouration?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. As a result of that, we have the information contained at tile 150, which is Dr Harkness intubating [Baby E] with a tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think he told us, did Dr Harkness, that this was at 23.45. [Baby E] was being ventilated in 100% oxygen, he was given further saline, and blood was taken for a clotting screen and a cross-match.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In terms of a clotting screen, if we can deal with that now, please, and if Mr Murphy would help me by putting up J2704. Are these the results of that screen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they are.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I am sure the jury know this without any explanation, but the tests being undertaken are those in the left-hand column, aren't they, PT and APTT?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The results are the next figures across as we read across?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then the ranges on the right-hand side are those that are given by the lab for the "normal" ranges, is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Each hospital has potentially a slightly different normal range, although they are around the same, but they may not be exact and may vary from hospital to hospital, but the hospital normal ranges tend to be adult normal ranges and, for some tests, children and neonates have a different normal range. But hospitals report an adult normal range, which is what this is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think Dr Harkness yesterday made reference to this, didn't he, although he wasn't able authoritatively at least to give us the normal ranges. I think you have again helped us by just researching that point; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. This is a common problem and because of that, the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health have published normal reference ranges for children and neonates. Sometimes the ranges for some tests vary according to age. Sometimes they vary according to gestation and sometimes they may be exactly the same as the adult range. So in order to help paediatricians, there is a published normal range and clotting studies feature in that. And the normal ranges for babies of gestation of between 30 and 36 weeks' gestation are given. I realised that [Baby E] was below 30 weeks' gestation, but there isn't a normal range for that, so I can only use the 30 to 36 week gestation range. And they also give a range from 0 to 7 days of life and from 7 days to 3 months of life, I think, and then from 3 months on. So there's a variety of different ranges of clotting values, depending on age and gestation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. Just dealing with these specific figures then. PT. What does --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That stands for prothrombin time. And obviously, in [Baby E], here it says 19.5. The upper limit of normal for his gestation and age produced by the Royal College I think from memory now is 18.1. So it's a little bit over, but... But not staggeringly so.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you like me to go on?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, yes. Let me -- you're clearly working from memory and I don't want to introduce errors. So your statement says that PT, prothrombin time, in preterm babies between 30 and 36 weeks at age 0 to 3 months is 8.5 to 17.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay, thank you.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's quite all right. You haven't got the paper in front of you. So what degree of elevation is the difference between 17 and 19.5 given those --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'd say it's marginal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the APTT, which I think is the -- go on, you say it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's easier to say PTT. It's the activated partial thromboplastin time. These two tests look at different parts of the clotting system and in [Baby E]'s case his result was 53.6
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: and, again, working from memory, but I'm sure you'll correct me, I think it's about 75.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Correct, well done.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So he's well within the range for his age and gestation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So just going back to the chronology if we may, [Dr C], we know, arrived at 00.25.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's what she records in the notes. And by 11 minutes later, at 00.36, no cardiac output could be detected from [Baby E] and his saturations were 50 to 60% in 100% oxygen and therefore full CPR was commenced.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We then know from Dr Wood's list precisely what was given and when in terms of resuscitation drugs.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You have recorded at 01.05 the information from [Baby E]'s blood gases, which is contained at tile 188; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you have also recorded that tragically [Baby E] didn't respond to resuscitation, resuscitative efforts were stopped at 01.23, and he was pronounced deceased at 01.40.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A post-mortem was not carried out. Do you have a view as to the advisability of that decision?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I do. I think that was a poor decision.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Post-mortems are carried out either when the clinician, in conjunction with the parents, agree that that is something that might be helpful to establish a cause of death or may add information to what the clinician believes is a cause of death and that requires the parents to give consent. But where one can't actually give a cause of death as a doctor you can't then sign a death certificate. So the case is referred to His Majesty's Coroner, who then decides whether a post-mortem should be carried out. And this was referred to His Majesty's Coroner. Unfortunately, a post-mortem wasn't carried out and I think that that was the wrong decision.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Whose decision is it? Is it the coroner's?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's the coroner's decision.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think you next refer to [Mother of Babies E & F]'s statement, in which [Mother of Babies E & F] recorded what she told us in effect, that at 9 pm she had seen her son in a distressed state.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And also that she had seen blood around his mouth.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You refer to the fact of her making a telephone call at 21.11 hours --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- and the absence of that material from the nursing record.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You also refer to Dr Harkness' statement about being called to review [Baby E] because of a dirty aspirate.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the fact that Dr Harkness had made an entry in the notes at 22.10, which we have now seen many times.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Taking all that information into account together with the evidence that you have heard over the last few days, did you reach a conclusion as to the condition of [Baby E] between his birth on 29 July and the time of the handover on the nursing shift at about 8 pm on the evening of 3 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, he was incredibly stable. He was fed, he was having skin-to-skin, he was incredibly stable and his blood tests accorded with that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Given the issues surrounding [Mother of Babies E & F]'s pregnancy, was [Baby E] at increased risk of NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, he was, because of the absent end-diastolic flow.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was his treatment managed appropriately following his birth at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In your experience, how does NEC present?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It has no single presenting feature, but it can present with feeding tolerance, it can present with temperature instability -- and some of these are very non-specific things, so they're not diagnostic of NEC. It can present with abdominal distension, abdominal pain if it's more severe. It can present with bloody stools.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It can present with a gastric perforation. So anything from very mild non-specific signs to -- if left untreated it goes on to be much more serious and then the signs and symptoms are more dramatic.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do babies go from being well one minute to very, very unwell within a matter of minutes or even a couple of hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not in my experience if they've got NEC, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You record at your paragraph 5.4 that the signs of NEC, which you have described, were not present in [Baby E]'s case; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You record that [Baby E] had been tolerating his feeds?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that he had passed meconium for the first time on 3 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think we have encountered meconium before, but could you just remind us what that means, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Meconium is the first faeces that babies pass in the first few days of life. It's slightly different from normal stool in that it's kind of black and tarry.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You record the fact that in all the examinations, so far as you could tell at the material time, [Baby E]'s abdomen was not tender, nor was it distended, and the two X-rays that were taken of him, of that area of him, showed no features of NEC.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Therefore, so far as the putative diagnosis of NEC was concerned, what view did you arrive at?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In my opinion, he did not have NEC.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Turning to what was recorded, your paragraph 6, in the time -- at 17.00 and 19.00 hours on 3 August, when [Baby E] was fed 2ml of milk, the aspirates were recorded as minimal.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Prior to the 21.00 hours feed, as the jury know, and they've seen this chart many times, on the fluid chart there is a 16 ml "mucky aspirate" aspirated from the nasogastric tube. In your experience, what does mucky aspirate mean?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It usually refers to a sort of brownish-green aspirate, so that's stomach juices plus any milk that may have been in the abdomen with -- maybe containing bile and sometimes containing flecks of blood. Altered blood goes brown, so it makes it kind of brown, I guess that's why it's termed "dirty" on occasion.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the context of a baby who'd been fed twice at 5 and 7 pm, had been fed 2ml and on each occasion there had been a minimal aspirate, what view did you take of this record that at 9 pm, before he'd been fed, there'd been a 16ml aspirate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It just struck me as being really odd and out of keeping with what had gone before. Clearly, you don't just take the volume of aspirate in isolation, you have to link it to his clinical condition, which had been fine, and he'd shown no signs of any gastrointestinal disturbance.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He had tolerated those feeds up until that point and had had no aspirate at all. So I was just at a loss to explain where this 16ml had come from, having had no aspirate before and having had nothing in his tummy for 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On the subject of bleeding being caused by a nasogastric tube, what is your experience -- I'm thinking now of the conversation that [Mother of Babies E & F] told us about with Lucy Letby. What is your experience of bleeding being caused by NGTs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As Dr Evans previously stated, these tubes are very fine and they're very soft and they're very flexible.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I could see that at least two attempts were made to put a nasogastric tube down, they were unsuccessful putting it into one nostril, but successfully put it into the other nostril. The fact of trying to place that tube in the nose can sometimes cause minor trauma to the delicate lining of the nose and you sometimes very get some very minor bleeding, very minor. I have never seen a baby haemorrhage or have blood around the mouth as a result of a nasogastric tube insertion, ever.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Looking at your paragraph 12, what view did you take as to the characterisation of the upper GI haemorrhage that [Baby E] exhibited at around 22.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Characterisation in terms of volume?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh, well, it appeared that he had a huge amount of haemorrhage at that point. Obviously, he vomited fresh blood and so we don't know the volume of that. But that's an extremely unusual feature, to vomit fresh blood. And then had an additional 14ml of fresh blood in the syringe attached to the nasogastric tube. And the combination of the previous volumes and this represents a substantial amount of this baby's blood volume.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think there was the further 13ml recorded at 23.00 hours; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. There was a further 13ml. If you add all that up, and I felt that was likely to be an underestimate because we don't know the volume of blood vomited or blood plus gastric content vomited, that represented over 25% of his blood volume.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think you're aware that at least one other expert in blood-related matters has considered whether or not [Baby E] had some sort of predisposition to bleeding; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And do you defer to her view so far as that is concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But in the absence of there being an "innocent"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: explanation for this bleeding, did you draw any conclusions?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Haemorrhage of this magnitude in neonates is vanishingly rare. I have never seen a baby haemorrhage, have a gastric haemorrhage, in this way. Babies do sometimes have gastric erosion and ulceration but it does not result in haemorrhage of this fashion. Nothing like losing 25% of your blood volume. So I was then trying to look for other possible causes for what I had never seen before and, on reviewing the literature, I came up with something very odd, of which there were only six recorded cases in neonates and obviously in the absence of a post-mortem I have no idea. But the world literature only has six cases.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that six cases in Chester or...?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: World literature.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the world?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the world ever recorded since it was first labelled in 1968.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just for our general education, what's that particular phenomenon known as?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's called Dieulafoy's lesion, and what is suggested is that it is a cause of -- can be a cause of major intestinal haemorrhage. Again the literature relates to adult practice rather than children's, but even then it's very rare and it's where there is an artery within the stomach wall, which is normally placed, but which has an increased calibre and therefore spontaneously haemorrhages as a result of some trauma, usually, or gastric erosion, so some sort of inflammatory process in the gut wall causes that artery to bleed and then there's catastrophic haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think really, I was clutching at straws because I reviewed the literature looking for something that could account for the extraordinary circumstance of this haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You say clutching at straws, were you trying to establish a malevolent cause or an innocent cause?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was just trying to establish an innocent cause, a pathological cause for this, because I've never seen it in my experience of neonatology.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You remark next on the abdominal discolouration recorded or described by Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Taking all those factors into account, did you reach an opinion as to why [Baby E] died when he did?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think [Baby E] died because of an air embolus. On that day he had the discolouration that was described by Dr Harkness, he suddenly collapsed where his previous clinical condition was not one where that was expected, and he did not respond to what was standard resuscitation. So on the basis of those things, on balance I thought he had an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In your view, did the bleeding contribute to his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think the bleeding made him unstable, but I don't think that was what caused his death.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And do you reject as a proposition the idea that [Baby E] had NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I do. [Baby E] didn't have NEC.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you wait there, please, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Bohin, you were provided with Dr Evans' reports in this case from the outset of your involvement, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've explained or been asked to explain that you're involved in something that's called a peer review; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In other words, almost a second opinion on what Dr Evans says?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's reviewing what Dr Evans has said and then forming my own opinion.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not going to disagree that there are things Dr Evans has said that you have not followed or endeavoured to follow, but I do suggest to you that you are prepared to support him in his conclusions where you feel you can, and that is your attitude. Do you agree or disagree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I totally disagree with that. I form my own opinions and I'm not simply going along with Dr Evans' opinions.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I suggest if Dr Evans had not -- if you hadn't received a report from Dr Evans suggesting air embolus in the case of [Baby E], you would never have come to a conclusion that that had anything to do with what took place, would you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby E], quite patently, died because of a catastrophic bleed, whatever the cause was. That was the cause of his death, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't believe so. I think he died of an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard that from your evidence he had lost about 25% of his blood volume at a point before CPR had even commenced.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard that when CPR did commence, the blood was, to use the words employed, pouring out of him.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All of which may have been or could have been a cause of his death, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not disputing the fact that he had a catastrophic haemorrhage, but I don't think that was what caused him to collapse and require CPR.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: From the clinical evidence that we have seen, the clinical notes, I suggest to you there is nothing in those that would have led you to conclude air embolus had Dr Evans not put that out there in the first place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I reviewed the notes and came to my own conclusions.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What we've seen in the notes in terms of discolouration is a reference to purple patches on the abdomen, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And also, separately, a reference to poor perfusion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Poor perfusion is what we might expect if a patient is hypoxic, in other words if there's been a decrease of oxygen, do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And there are a number of reasons why there may be poor perfusion, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And bleeding is one of them, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But he had maintained his blood pressure at that point, so bleeding can be, but you wouldn't take that in isolation, you would look at the other parameters and actually his blood pressure was maintained, so that alone wouldn't have accounted for the poor perfusion in a child with a normal blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As I asked Dr Harkness yesterday, blood pressure actually is the last sign to go, isn't it, in fact?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is, but it was normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A colour change where it simply says "purple patches on abdomen" may have any number of explanations, mightn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but I can't think of other explanations that will fit with this clinical picture.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In terms of the collapse at 23.40, [Baby E] was stabilised within a relatively short period of time, wasn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And indeed, any discolouration at all had gone by the time [Dr C] attended, the consultant?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She didn't note it, so yes, I suppose it must have gone.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She didn't record it if it was present.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in her view, it seemed that [Baby E] was stable at that point when she was there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So we have [Baby E] stable at some point around about 00.25, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then, according to the evidence of Dr Harkness, right in front of their eyes, some time after that, [Baby E] collapsed again?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That collapse doesn't involve any question of discolouration, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That collapse is when blood began to pour out of him when CPR was performed upon him, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Blood came out because CPR was being performed, because he had an ongoing gastrointestinal haemorrhage, and if that's the case and you're performing chest compressions by definition you will cause blood to leave the stomach and come out of the nose and mouth.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So in other words, at the time of that collapse, there must have been quite profuse bleeding inside him, that second collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I... I don't think -- we don't know the volume, so I have no idea of knowing because I don't know the volume. But blood was coming out of his nose and mouth is all we know.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It was described as "pouring out of him" as they were doing chest compressions?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that must be from a bleed inside him, mustn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, he had an ongoing gastrointestinal haemorrhage, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You mentioned you received the report of Owen Arthurs, the paediatric radiologist, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The surefire way of identifying an air embolus in life would be to be able to see the air in the heart, wouldn't it, or around the region of the heart, don't you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. But it is a cause, isn't it?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that may indicate some underlying problem; do you agree?

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "not necessarily", that means it may?

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Stress is capable of raising acidity within the stomach, isn't it, even in a neonate, physical stress?

blocks.text: [Baby E] wasn't under any physical stress. I'm not aware that stress can increase acidity in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When I say physical stress, I mean whatever it is that leads to the increase in blood glucose, if it's a stressor, that may increase acidity, gastric acidity, mightn't it?

blocks.text: I don't know, I don't know that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Increased acidity in the stomach can cause erosion or ulceration of the stomach lining, can't it?

blocks.text: During her interview on 4 July 2018, Lucy Letby did recall caring for [Baby E]. blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She didn't know why there was no entry about the blood on his mouth. The amount must only have been small with mucus in it as she would not class that as something to be overly concerned about.

blocks.text: Lucy Letby denied intending or causing any harm to [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON
